> 「善男子、善女人，发阿耨多罗三藐三菩提心，云何应住？云何降伏其心？」……「实无有法，发阿耨多罗三藐三菩提心者。」……「如来者，即诸法如义。」

The seventeenth section repeats the question from section two, word for word.

须菩提 asks again: one who has aroused the mind of awakening — where should it abide, how should it be subdued?

The repetition is deliberate, and the answer this time is different. Not a new technique; the same instruction, but with the ground removed from under it.

## What changed between section two and section seventeen

In section two, the question was asked by someone who had not yet heard the answer. In section seventeen, it is asked after fifteen sections of dismantling — after merit has been emptied, after marks have been cancelled, after the body of the Buddha has been denied as evidence.

So the answer can now be stated in its final form: 实无有法，发阿耨多罗三藐三菩提心者. There is no dharma that arouses the mind of awakening.

Not: nobody arouses it. Not: arousing it is pointless. What is denied is a *thing* — an entity called "the one who has aroused the mind", stored somewhere, to be maintained and protected.

## 如来者，即诸法如义

The definition of the Tathāgata given here is the sutra's most compressed sentence: the Tathāgata is the suchness of all dharmas.

如 — thus, as it is, without addition or subtraction. Not a person who is thus; the thusness itself.

Which is why the word 如来 can be read as 如 + 来: appearing as it actually is. Not someone who arrived from somewhere.

## 无实无虚

Again the pair, and again it does the load-bearing work.

无实: the awakening cannot be grasped as an object obtained. 无虚: the causal order, the work of liberating beings, the effects of conduct — none of it is nullified.

The book's phrasing: things are entirely functional and entirely ungraspable. The two clauses are not a compromise between two positions; they are one position, stated in a way that blocks both exits.

## 一切法皆是佛法 has a guardrail

The section says all dharmas are buddha-dharma. The sentence is regularly flattened into "everything is sacred, therefore nothing is", which is the opposite of what it says.

The book's guardrail: what makes a dharma buddha-dharma is being seen as to its suchness, free of marks. Not the phenomenon itself being holy, and certainly not the claim that harmful conduct is dharma. Causes and effects remain exact.

## 无我法

And then the last turn of the screw: even 无我 must not be held as a dharma.

Which catches the reader who has followed this far and built a position out of the demolition — the person who now says "there is no self" as an established fact, and defends it.

The sutra's final move in this section is to remove that too. Not because the statement is false, but because a statement held is a mark, and the whole path has been the undoing of marks.

## The test

Say the sentence "there is no self" out loud, and then check what is saying it.

If there is someone there, pleased with the sentence, holding it as an achievement — the seventeenth section has just described that position, and then declined to leave it standing.

The question from section two is still the question. What changed is that there is now less to put it down on.
